sections.text: Every value in Rust has a type. Scalar types hold a single value: integers, floating-point numbers, booleans and characters.
Integers come in signed (i8, i16, i32, i64, i128) and unsigned (u8 up to u128) sizes. i32 is the default. usize is used for counts and indexes.
Floats are f64 (the default) and f32. bool is true or false. char is a single Unicode character in single quotes:
Dividing two integers drops the remainder, so 7 / 2 is 3. Use floats when you need the fraction.
Rust never mixes number types on its own. You can't multiply an integer by a float, even when the answer seems obvious. Convert one of them first with as:
items as f64 turns the integer 3 into the float 3.0, so both sides of * are f64 and the program prints 7.5.

Coming from another language: there are no automatic number conversions in Rust, not even from i32 to i64. If an integer overflows while the program runs, it stops with an error. That's what happens in this app and in cargo run (a debug build). Release builds skip that check and wrap around silently, unless you turn overflow checks on.

Coming from another language: number literals can carry a type suffix, like 5u8 or 2.5f32. usize is as wide as a pointer, so 64 bits on most machines today. A char is 4 bytes, because it holds any Unicode character, not a single byte.
The _ in 1_250 is just for readability, like a comma in 1,250.

exercise.prompt: This program doesn't compile because total is a float and count is an integer, and Rust won't divide one by the other. Convert count to f64 with as so it prints: 2.5
